segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Thank you. Honourable Ministers, Excellencies, representatives of development partners, leaders from the private sector, representatives of financial institutions, young entrepreneurs, ladies and gentlemen, good morning.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: I'm here on behalf of Honourable Minister of Agriculture and Animal Resources, Dr. Tresfo Ndalmenye, who couldn't be here despite his strong wish, but due to other concurrent commitments, he delegated me to represent him here. So I will read his speech verbatim. It is a great pleasure and honour to join you today as we gather around an important and timely theme, buy from youth in agriculture.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: First and foremost, I wish to commend the young women and men who have chosen agriculture not simply as an occupation, but as an opportunity to innovate, create businesses, generate employment, and contribute to the development of our country. Your presence here demonstrates that agriculture is not an activity of the past. It is a sector of opportunity, innovation, entrepreneurship, and prosperity.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, agriculture remains a strategic pillar of Rwanda's economy, food and nutrition security, rural transformation, and overall socioeconomic development. However, transforming agriculture requires more than increasing production. It requires building a competitive, market-oriented and resilient agricultural sector that creates value, generates decent jobs, and connects producers to profitable markets.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: This is where young people have a critical role to play because the youth bring fresh ideas, technological skills, creativity, ambition, and an entrepreneurial mindset. They are introducing new approaches to farming, livestock production, agro-processing, mechanization, irrigation, digital agriculture, logistics, packaging, and agricultural marketing, to mention but a few. Across our country, young entrepreneurs are demonstrating that agriculture can be modern, profitable, and attractive.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: They are producing quality agricultural products, developing innovative solutions, creating businesses, and they are producing quality agricultural produce and providing employment opportunities for other young people. We must recognize, support, and celebrate these efforts. Distinguished guests, the theme for today's gathering, Buy from Youth in Agriculture, carries a powerful message.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: It is a call to move beyond encouraging young people to participate in agriculture towards actively creating markets for the products and services they provide. We often tell young people to become entrepreneurs, establish agricultural businesses, increase production, and embrace innovation. But we must also ask ourselves an important question.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Are we ready to buy from them? Are our institutions ready to procure their products? Are supermarkets, hotels, restaurants, processors, and distributors ready to source from youth-led enterprises? Are financial institutions ready to finance businesses that have secured markets and demonstrated potential? Are consumers ready to recognize the quality and value of products made by young entrepreneurs? Buying from young agripreneurs is not charity. It is an investment in business, innovation, employment, and the future of our agricultural sector. When we buy from a young farmer, we strengthen production.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: When we buy from a youth-led agro-processing enterprise, we support value addition. When we purchase agricultural services from young innovators, we encourage technology and entrepreneurship. And when we consistently create markets for youth-led agricultural businesses, we contribute to sustainable employment and inclusive economic growth.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, to make this commitment meaningful, I wish to highlight five areas where we must strengthen our collective efforts. First, expand market access for youth-led agricultural enterprises. There is a need to form structured market linkages, contract farming, aggregation, arrangements, and long-term supply agreements so that young entrepreneurs should not invest in the production without a clear understanding of market requirements and demand.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: There is also a need to promote quality standards and value addition. There's a need to encourage young entrepreneurs to invest in improvements, production practices, both service handling, food safety, quality assurance, packaging, branding, processing, and certification. We need to improve also access to finance and investment.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: There is a need to strengthen collaboration between financial institutions, development partners, investment funds, and agricultural stakeholders to develop financial products that respond to the realities of youth-led agricultural enterprises. Harnessing innovation and technology. The future of agriculture will increasingly depend on innovation and the effective use of technology.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Therefore, there is a need to encourage young people to take advantage of digital platforms, modern agricultural technologies, irrigation mechanization, improved seeds, livestock technologies, climate-smart agriculture, and data-driven solutions. Building partnerships and changing perceptions about agriculture. Creating opportunities for youth in agriculture is a shared responsibility.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Government, the private sector, financial institutions, cooperatives, development partners, research institutions, and consumers, we must work together. As the ministry responsible for agriculture and animal resources, we recognize that creating an enabling environment for youth participation in agriculture requires coordinated action across the entire agricultural value chain. Our efforts must continue to focus on increasing productivity, improving access to productive resources, strengthening agricultural markets, promoting value addition, attracting private investment, and supporting entrepreneurship.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Today, I wish to make a special appeal to all buyers and market actors represented here. Do not simply applaud young agricultural entrepreneurs. Give them opportunities.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Do not only encourage them to produce. Establish purchasing relationships with them. Do not only speak about youth empowerment.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Demonstrate it through procurement, investment, mentorship, and market partnerships. To our young agripreneurs, my message is equally clear. Be innovative.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Be ambitious. Understand your markets. Produce according to quality standards.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: Build strong business relationships. Embrace technology and continuously improve your products and services. Do not be afraid to start small, but always think about growing into competitive and sustainable enterprises.

segments.speaker: Dr. Patrick Karangwa · DG Agriculture Modernization, MINAGRI
segments.text: The market rewards quality, reliability, consistency, and innovation. Let us, therefore, work together to build an agricultural sector in which young people are not merely beneficiaries of development programs, but active drivers of economic transformation. I thank you for your kind attention.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you so much, Dr. Patrick, for those warm remarks from the Ministry of Agriculture and Animal Resources. segments.text: Honorable Ministers, distinguished government representatives, UN colleagues, development partners, the private sector, youth from different parts of Africa and everyone, please allow me to stand on all the existing protocols. segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: It's my pleasure to join so many young entrepreneurs, private sector actors, financial institutions and partners committed to advancing youth-led agribusiness in Mother Africa and in Rwanda in particular. At the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations, together with the World Food Programme and across the UN systems here in Rwanda and in many other parts of Africa, we see young people not simply as beneficiaries. We see them as entrepreneurs, innovators, job creators and leaders who are already shaping the future of our agri-food systems.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: This is particularly important for Rwanda and indeed for many other parts of Africa. We have a young and increasingly connected population, while the agri-sector and the wider agri-food systems remain critical to livelihoods, food security and economic transformation. But when we talk about jobs in agriculture, we must look beyond farming.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Opportunities exist across the entire value chain. Input supply, mechanization, irrigation, aggregation, processing, packaging, transport, marketing, finance and export. And digitalization is also opening even more more opportunities in the agri-sector.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Young people working in the sector should embrace digital technology and innovation to raise their productivity and even earn more from the farming and related activities. They can also lead that change for others by linking farmers to markets, offering digital advisory services, widening access to finance and markets, market information and building new technologies. They can also help make farmers more productive.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: They can make agriculture sector more productive, competitive, profitable for everyone in the value chain. This is especially important in a country where land is very much limited. Rwanda's agricultural future must be about producing more and better with the resources we have, adding value, reducing losses, embracing technology and connecting farmers to profitable markets.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: FAO, WFP and other UN systems in Rwanda and in many parts of Africa are already supporting and promoting young people, especially young women and men from rural communities and towns. We want to help these young people become entrepreneurs and agents of food systems transformation and connect their ideas and businesses to markets, finance, technology and investment. But we have learned an important lesson.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Training young people is not enough. A young entrepreneur may have excellent skills and an excellent product, but without access to finance and crucially without a buyer, that business cannot grow or create jobs. This is why buying from youth is so important.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: We must move from asking what can young people produce to asking what are we prepared to buy from the young people, because markets create businesses, businesses create, generate income and successful business creates jobs and that's what we need in Rwanda and in many other parts of Africa. This therefore requires all of us, government, creating enabling environment, financial institutions providing appropriate financing, the young and the private sector opening supply chains and the development partners helping young entrepreneurs grow and compete. So let's today's youth market lab be more than other conversations with youth.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Let young people and young entrepreneurs meet buyers, let good ideas meet investors and let those connections lead to contracts, investment and jobs. FAO, WFB and the entire UN system in Rwanda remains committed to an inclusive, green and increasingly digital agri-food systems in which young people are not standing on the margins, but are leading the transformation. If we believe young people are the future of Africa's food systems, we must invest in them, partner with them, open market for them and importantly buy from them.

segments.speaker: FAO Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Excellencies, Honorable Ministers, Representatives of African Union, Representatives of UNDP, distinguished private sector leaders, young entrepreneurs and innovators, ladies and gentlemen, I am very pleased to join you here in Kigali at the YouthConnekt Africa Summit 2026 and to contribute to this important conversation on buy from youth, turning green livelihood into green market. Let me begin by recognizing the Government of Rwanda, YouthConnekt Africa, UNDP South Sudan, the African Union and all the partners for bringing together government, development institution, the private sector and young people to advance Africa development agenda.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: I am particularly pleased that South Sudan is now part of the YouthConnekt Africa family. We see this platform as an opportunity to strengthen our national youth development agenda, build partnership and connect our young people to opportunities across the continent. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, Africa green transition is an economic opportunity, a job agenda and an opportunity to transform the livelihood of millions of young Africans.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: For example, for South Sudan, this opportunity is enormous. Our country has vast agricultural potential, fertile land, significant water resource, livestock and diverse natural resources. Agriculture can drive economy, diversification, food security, employment and sustainable development.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Yet, despite this potential, South Sudan still depends heavily on important food. We spend more than 800 million annually on food import, while much of our agricultural potential remains underutilized. For Africa, this presents fundamental economic opportunity.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Imagine what could happen if we invest more in our young farmer, agro-processes, agriculture, technology, entrepreneur, irrigation specialist, renewable energy innovators and local manufacturing business. Imagine if more of the food consumed in our market were processed, produced, packaged and supplied by young enterprise. We would not strengthen food security.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: We would not only strengthen food security, we would create jobs, keep wealth in our community, reduce dependence on import and build a more resilient economy. Our challenge, therefore, is not lack of potential. It's how to connect that potential to productive investment, skill, technology, infrastructure, finance and reliable markets.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, the government of South Sudan recognizes that young people must be at the center of this transformation. Through our partnership with UNDP South Sudan and development partners, we are creating opportunity for youth through market-linked agricultural skills, vocational training, entrepreneurship development and start-up support. We run initiatives to promote youth participation in agriculture, livestock management, irrigation and climate smart agriculture, while strengthening rural producer organization, cooperative and agricultural value chain.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: However, we must go further. We must move beyond supporting young people to produce food and agriculture and agricultural products. We must ensure that they can process, package, transport, market and sell their product competitively.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Our ambition must be to move from supporting young people to grow crops to supporting them to build agriculture enterprise. Distinguished delegates, for South Sudan and Africa, I believe five areas require particular attention. First, investing in climate smart agriculture and green skill.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: We must equip young people with knowledge and technology to adopt climate resilient farming, sustainable livestock production, irrigation, renewable energy and environmentally sustainable production method. Second, connecting youth enterprises to finance and productive resources. Youth entrepreneurs need more than training.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: They need affordable finance, access to land, irrigation infrastructure, equipment, improved seed technology and business development services. Third, we must create market for youth-owned businesses. This is the central message of today's discussion.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Government must become deliberate in creating opportunity for youth entrepreneurs to supply goods and services. We should encourage public institutions, private companies, supermarkets, hotels, schools and other major buyers to source products from qualified youth-owned enterprises. We must strengthen local procurement, promote business information, formalization, improve market information and connect youth producers to national, regional and continental value chain.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Fourth, investing in agriculture value, additional infrastructure. We need youth enterprise in food processing, packaging, storage, transportation, coal chain system, agricultural mechanization and digital agricultural services. Investment in rural energy, irrigation and storage facility will be essential to reduce harvesting losses and connecting producer to consumer.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: And fifth, strengthening partnership and regional trade. We must work together with development partners, financial institution, university and the private sector to mobilize investment and technical experts. We must also leverage the African continental free trade area to connect youth-owned enterprise to regional market and new business opportunity.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, as government, we recognize that our responsibility goes beyond advocating for youth. We must help create an enabled environment where they can participate in the economy, access opportunity and contribute to national development. We invite development partner to invest in youth-led green enterprise, not only in training program.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: We invite financial institution to develop accessibility, but accessible financing product for youth enterprise and youth entrepreneurs. We invite the private sector to open its supply chain and procurement opportunity to youth-owned business. And to our young people, do not limit your ambition to seeking employment, looking at the opportunity around you, your land, your water, our agricultural resource and our community, others in our most possible for innovation and enterprise.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, let us make buy from youth a commitment that shape how we invest, procure, trade and build our economy. The future of the green economy must be youth-driven, market-oriented and build on country immense agricultural potential. Now, I would like to take this opportunity to tell our African head of state and ministers that we have to take this from at heart.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: We have to commit. Commitment is the key here. Without commitment, this one cannot go forward.

segments.speaker: Undersecretary for Youth, South Sudan
segments.text: Thank you and God bless Africa.

Tell us, inspire. Africa has encouraged young entrepreneurs to create businesses, to innovate, create jobs and solve existing problems. We have done that.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: But I'm still wondering, the people who are encouraging young entrepreneurs to create businesses are the same people when the product is out, are already ready to buy from someone else. Ladies and gentlemen, a good afternoon. My name is Nabaka Sandra.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I'm the CEO and co-founder of Sendi AI Technologies, a tech company from Uganda and a proud GoGetters grand prize winner 2026. At Sendi AI, we have developed technologies combining soil moisture sensors, precision solar irrigation systems and artificial intelligence. We have also tried to bring access these technologies to the community through seven groups.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We are not alone. Across Africa, there are a lot of young innovators who are bringing solutions to the globe. But one question, who is buying these solutions when they are already out? When it is time for the contracts, there is always a challenge and a change in the programme.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: People tend to ask, we need international experts. We need a company with a five-year experience. So tell me, how is a company like Sendi AI going to be out there if no one is willing to give the first year contract? How is a young company going to gain the first five years of experience that you have without giving a chance to a one-year contract? Sometimes I feel like we are going to be awarded on stages, not to be given the contract.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I'm so proud and it was a beautiful moment for us that we won the grand prize from GoGetters. But unfortunately, the awards do not pay engineers, do not take those irrigations to farms, but customers do. Who is going to buy from us? If the people from the government, local innovators, project partners don't give us chances.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: To my fellow young entrepreneurs, we also have a responsibility. When we see the opportunities, let us always try to keep the bridge to deliver and also to keep the friendship with the buyers so that they always return. Africa has spent years asking its young people to build.

segments.speaker: Sandra · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We have really built. But who is buying from us? Another question is, there is no longer a question that whether African youth can build or they cannot. The question is, who is going to buy from what we have built? Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you so much, Sandra. Thank you so much for sharing your entrepreneurial journey. I now call Jean-Pierre Mouniamana.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Jean-Pierre Mouniamana, you're next. And Jean-Pierre Mouniamana is representing Smart Farm Solutions Limited. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: Thank you for having me here. My name is Jean-Pierre Mouniamana and I am a Rwandan agripreneur and I am managing director of Smart Farm Solutions Company Limited. After completing my college, I had ambition to become entrepreneur.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: But becoming an entrepreneur, the dream itself, it was easy. But down there to become an entrepreneur, it was challenging. I was like somebody like you.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: I had no connections. I had not any rich family who can give me a capital. But I had a powerful skills and knowledge.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: I did agriculture from the college. That was only the powerful tool I had. So after through the gigs and casual jobs I had, I started savings.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: And after, by using the savings, I started this company called Smart Farm Solutions Company Limited focusing on livestock farming, particularly pig farming production. To me, I'm a pig farmer. But also, starting a company, it was not my biggest challenge.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: My biggest challenge came after starting the company or a farm. To find the market, it was a big challenge for me. And as an agripreneur, I sat down and asked myself, how am I going to survive? My pigs are growing and is approaching to the selling age.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: And I don't have any reliable customer. How am I going to survive? They are eating, they are consuming my money, but I don't know where I'm going to sell the pigs. And I sat down and asked myself, what is the opportunities I have? What are the choices I have? I mean, what can I do to help the customers? As a generation Z, our powerful tool is to use social media.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: Everyone knows how to use social media. We always scroll or post our vibes. So I used to say that, what if I can just post my pigs and I can try to get the customers from my social media? I did and it works.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: Within a days, the customers and the inquiries started to come in and they started receiving the inquiries of the piglets, mature pigs for meat. And the strategy of marketing through my social media works. And some of you know me as agronome on different social media.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: So after getting the clients of my pigs, I also started to sell for others because I had a few pigs and the clients came bigger. But the challenge today for us as youth, we will not all market through social media. We are not all good by using social media.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: There is another way to have access to the market. That's why I want to appeal to the policy makers here. That's why I want to appeal to the organizational supporters here.

segments.speaker: Jean-Pierre · Smart Farm Solutions
segments.text: I want to thank you for the support for the youth of today. But I want also to ask you and appeal you to also include the youth to have access to market. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you very much, Jean-Pierre Murakose. So after Jean-Pierre, now allow me to call Claudine Kamanzi who is representing Forest for Life. Claudine, over to you.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: Have you ever started a business thinking of your waiting customers? So many customers coming to buy your product, but again, you wait for so long and then you find none is coming. Imagine waking up in the morning, watering your trees or your product, taking care of them. But again, you find that no one is there to support you.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: You wait for the customers for one day, second day, even the weeks pass. Then you find that your product are growing rather than the customers. Well, that was my story.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: Good afternoon, everyone. My name is Kamanzi Claudine, standing here. To my fellow young people, hello, everyone.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: Three years ago, I and my colleague, we started Forest for Life initiative where we're producing free trees, native indigenous trees. But we're waiting for the customers as young as any other person who is in the business. And sometimes we thought that the customers throughout different marketing things we did, we participate in different platforms.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: But again, getting customers for our product was not easy. We said that, but if we're not getting customers, but if we can try to contribute to our community, we take our trees, we give it to the communities, hoping that at least they can use it to provide the fruit to the families. Slowly by slowly, people in our community start marketing our product.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: We get people who trust us. We get to hear people who encourage us. We see the people who connected us to the opportunities.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: To the partners, investors, and financial institutions, I want to ask you, when you see young people bringing a business idea or the person who is doing a business, do you see them as a risk or possibilities? To young fellow, young entrepreneurs in the room, when you see the business, if your business is not working, what do you do? Do you think even your communities, because your community can be the next customers? I want to encourage everyone, if you are here, if you see young people doing something, producing, having a product, please encourage him or her and remember to buy from him or her. That journey with my colleague, we learned that trees need to be grown up, needs to be watered, but a business needs strategy to prosper. So that means that for every young entrepreneur in the room, it's always good to have strategies, thinking not going beyond for your communities.

segments.speaker: Claudine Kamanzi · Forest for Life
segments.text: Try to find different opportunities that is in the way. Thank you so much. Remember to buy from the youth.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you so much, Claudine, and thank you so much. We will buy from youth, definitely. As we continue our journey of youth-led innovation, I would like to welcome Smart Israel, who is our next speaker.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Distinguished guests, honourable ministers, young people from all across Africa, my name is Smart Israel and I'm the founder of Smarter.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I want to start by telling a very short story. The first time I walked into a college classroom, my facilitator asked me, what is your mission? And that was the first time I heard anything of that sort. And so I said, I don't know what my mission is.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Two days later, I realized that it was a requirement for me to pass the semester in order to move to the next semester. And so I said, okay, I'm going to come up with a mission. So I used two things.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: One, I asked, what is the most pressing issue in my community? And it was food insecurity. Secondly, I asked myself, what am I most passionate about? It was technology. And so by the end of the week, I went back to my facilitator and I said, my mission is to use technology at the intersection of entrepreneurship to create empowering experiences for people with a focus on food system.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: And that was where my journey began. Eventually, this mission built what I call Smartel. Smartel is an agri-tech company that builds smart hydroponic system.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We call it farm in a box. The idea of farm in a box is that you're able to feed an entire farm inside a box and transport it from one place to the other. And you're able to grow food using this hydroponic system that can be assembled and dismantled, that is powered by solar and IoT.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: That was the beginning of my journey. And I just want to share two things. Number one, how we went from zero to where we are today, and why you should bet on young people.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Starting Smartel, I had nothing, just an idea, a passion, and two things I really like. Number one, to solve the problem in my community. And number two, using technology to make that happen.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I realized I had three key intangible assets. And that's what I want to talk about. Number one is the skill and knowledge.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I asked myself, what do I know about the problem I want to solve? What do I know about this industry that no one else knows about? What do I know about the people that I want to serve that no other person knows about? Something that is backed by evidence and research. That was the first question I asked myself. And I realized that there are over 200 million people across Africa who struggle with access to food due to climate change and its impacts.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: And that began my journey. The second question was, how do I leverage relationships and networks to solve this problem? And so I asked myself, who are the people that care about this solution as much as I do? Who are the stakeholders? FAO, UNDP, World Food Program, Africa Food System. Those were the stakeholders.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Lastly, collaboration. Africans are some of the most competitive individuals on Earth. And there's a place for competition.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: But I realized that we must collaborate in order to build systems that last. Because even personal success cannot insulate you from the failures of your society. And with these three things, I was able to start off my journey.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We got funding from people who care. We got supported by the World Food Program, including Google, through the Google for Startup Accelerator Program, and now recently, GoGetters, by being the grand prize meal winner for the GoGetters Prize 2026. And that kicked off my journey.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Today, we've been able to serve thousands of farmers through our smart hydroponic system across Africa. And we're on track to raise over a million dollars in funding to expand this solution. There are two key lessons here.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Number one is that you must be willing to use what you don't have, or what you have rather, to get what you don't have. And these are the intangible assets I spoke about. Lastly, to the investors in the room, young people are capable.

segments.speaker: Smart Israel · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Young people are willing if you just bet on them and buy from youth. Thank you so much.

segments.text: Thank you very much, Israel.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: Hello everyone.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: Good afternoon. So, now I'm going to ask you a question and I hope you will answer. Imagine a farmer is planning for the next season and the land is ready.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: And even this family is counting for the harvesting. Also, a farmer is ready to work. But what happens when crop inputs, seeds, fertilizers and crop protection, even post-harvest equipments are not label accessible? The answer is yes.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: The farmer will start the season with disadvantages. My name is Danny Akizimana. I'm the founder of AgriMark Ltd.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: AgriMark Ltd simply means agriculture with market orientation. We access those challenges through providing farmers with inputs, fertilizers, even post-harvest equipments by a local agriculture inputs hub whereby we work with 4,000 farmers because we are now promoting farming with business oriented. And now we have a target of improving the numbers that we are working with.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: We are now looking forward to work with 10,000 farmers. And this initiative will help a farmer to access the market and then it will also reduce the losses of post-harvest.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: As we know in my region, there is a huge production of vegetables. That's why.

segments.text: Are you done? Yes? Oh, the microphone. Okay, sorry. Technical team would like to have your support, please, on the microphones.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: Thank you. Dear youth, investors and partners, let's work together and invest in agriculture for tomorrow's food. Through Agri-Mark Ltd, the farmer learn and farmer connect and also farmer grow.

segments.speaker: Danny Akizimana · AgriMark Ltd
segments.text: Let's buy from youth. I love you. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: What happens when a young farmer grow a crop, invest their money and finally get a good harvest but has no reliable market or way outside their product? Good morning, everyone.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I'm Shimo Yvette Umurielwa. I'm the founder and managing director of Farmisa Ltd, a youth-led agribusiness that is based here in Rwanda. I'm passionate about agriculture, especially agriculture that sustains our soil, protects the environment and the people who depend on it.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We are involved in crop production and vermicomposting where we grow crops like potatoes, vegetables like broccoli and beetroot. We do this with much integration of ecological approach and promoting sustainable farming practices that aim to keep our soil healthy. Today, we are now able to serve over 300 customers at the end of the season.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: The work that I'm doing today was inspired by what I learned and what I observed around me. With my background of soil science and natural resources management, I became increasingly concerned about the decline of our soil fertility and how agricultural practices are affecting our environment. It is when I started to think about the resources we already have around us.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: We already have those kitchen wastes, we already have those agricultural residual and biodegradable wastes we use to throw away as a waste. And I started to think beyond of that, where today in Farmisa Ltd, we maximize the use of all those kitchen wastes into vermicomposting, a nutrient-rich fertilizer that is there to improve the fertility of our soil and help farmers to get a good and high-quality yield. But as we continue this journey, there are some challenges we are facing until today.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: And that challenge is access to market. There are some times we grow a crop, we get a good harvest as we expected, but when it comes to time of selling, finding reliable market, or getting access to buyers who can purchase our product in the quantity that we need, it became very, very big challenges for us. And sometimes we end up selling our product at lower cost because we are afraid of getting a loss.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Learning from that challenge, I didn't overlook of them. I came up with this idea where we are now currently developing e-commerce platform, where that platform is going to connect young farmers to the market, to the potential buyers who can purchase their product in the quantity they need. The young farmers will be having a room to share the information of the product that are available so that the buyers can directly connect with them.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: For us, that platform, it is like our starting point. Looking ahead, the next five years, we need to put farmers are limited to the point who will be having a reliable market agreement, like contract farming opportunities. We have a goal to serve over 1,000 customers at the end of every season.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: I have also realized that this challenge of access to market, it is not my own challenge. It is a challenge we share in common as young farmers. That is why it will be our greatest opportunity if we could have access to the contract farming and get some mentorship opportunities in marketing so that we can get to understand our buyers, getting the knowledge about negotiating the price.

segments.speaker: Yvette · youth entrepreneur
segments.text: Thank you so much for having me. Let's make buy from you a reality because when you buy from you, you are investing in the future. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: Good morning, everyone. Let me start by asking a simple question.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: How many of you believe that a cow can change someone's future? I hope the positive answer comes to your mind. But with technology, it can transform the entire livestock value chain. I'm among the people whose parents sold a cow and milk to pay the school fees.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: And I also know some people take cows as an animal. But for me, cow represents education, opportunity, sacrifice and hope. As a veterinary doctor, I know the struggles of the farmers.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: I know how the farmers work in the morning, take care of their cow, produce milk and depend on each and every litre of milk to support their family. Without taking much of the time, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Festo Ndaisenga.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: I'm a veterinary doctor, a managing director of Gemura Solutions Ltd. I started this company since 2024. This company is mainly focused on the milk value chain.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: I developed the software called Gemura Software, it's a data analytics platform. I saw the problems the farmers are facing. The farmers do not only need to produce milk, they also need the market, access to finance and opportunity to grow.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: After I developed the system since 2024, that time I was back in Israel, where I got the skills from the farming. After I got here in our country, I initiated this initiative so that the farmers can have reliable data to access to the market, so that the data can be shared to the government to take a policy or decision that works for the livestock farmers. The system I tested since 2021 for one milk collection centre, so in 2026 I started to expand.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: Look where are we now. We have 83 milk collection centres that are using our system. What are the milk collection centres using our system? First, they record the milk delivered to the milk collection centres, they record the milk sold to the buyers, they record the milk rejections and some reasons and also they regenerate the payroll through the system and the management as well.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: So as of now, as I said, 93 milk collection centres across the country, out of 146 remaining three to cover across the country and also it is in 20 districts in the country. So now we have 3,000 cooperative members of livestock farmers onboarded on the system. We have 1.5 billion running farms transacted in the system and also I can track the milk rejections, I can track the milk aggregated, I can track the people who are active or not active.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, for the youth participant coming from abroad, the system is replicable. We can also expand it to your country. For financial institutions, I have a transaction, I have data for the farmers, join me to help the farmers to access to the finance because the data we have, it gives the value to the farmers.

segments.speaker: Festo · Gemura Solutions
segments.text: For government institutions, I have the data, the milk aggregated, the milk sold, the milk rejections and some reasons. I'm willing to share the data to the government so that they can make a policy that works for the farmers. Thank you so much.
