segments.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. So I'm now going to call Olivia Awuokini who is representing Econacy.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: So Olivia, please, same rule, one minute. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: All protocols observed. My name is Olivia Awuokini. I'm the founder and managing director.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: And we are a biomaterial startup based in Nairobi, Kenya. And basically what we do, we take agricultural pineapple waste and convert it into a more sustainable alternative to hide leather. So as you all know, for a long time, the leather industry has been reliant on animal skins as its primary source of raw materials.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: And traditional leather turning depends on is environmentally unsustainable and depends on toxic chemicals like chromium. And at the same time, in my home country, back in Kenya, we produce over 80 million tons of agricultural pineapple waste annually. So my team and I asked ourselves one question, what if the waste of one industry can actually become a raw material for the next? And we did exactly that.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: We've partnered with over 100 pineapple farmers in Kenya to convert their waste into a sustainable material that feels and performs just like animal leather, like this bag I'm holding over here. Believe it or not, it's made from pineapple waste. And we have moved past the idea stage.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: We are currently serving over 20 leather brands in Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria. And we are doing over $200,000 in revenue annually. So my call to you this afternoon is to buy from African youth, because when you buy from us, you're investing in the future of Africa.

segments.speaker: Olivia · Econacy
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you so much, Olivia. And thank you so much for inviting us for buying from you.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: The last one, not the least, is Josiane Mujawaiyesu. Josiane, where are you? Yes. Representing Amazing Insects Limited.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Josiane, the floor is yours and you have one minute. Thank you. A round of applause, yes.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: Thank you. Good afternoon to everyone. My name is Josiane Mujawaiyesu.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: I am a CEO and founder of Amazing Insects Limited, an agribusiness company, based in Uganda, transforming organic waste into organic fertilizer. My journey started when I was young. I have been always interested in insects.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: After getting an opportunity to study entomology in master's, I found that there are incredible worms and black soldier fly larvae transforming organic waste into organic fertilizer and animal feeds. In Uganda, based on the National Institute of Statistical Agriculture, over 75% of farmers face an acidic and aluminum toxicity problem, which reduces organic fertilizer and crop productivity. At the same time, we generate that quantity of organic waste that becomes an environmental problem.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: And farmers depend highly on chemical organic fertilizer. At Amazing Insects Limited, we turned this challenge into our opportunity. We use locally available organic waste and worms and black soldier fly larvae to convert organic waste into organic fertilizer.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: And we use soil and pH meter technology to monitor and keep product quality and safety. In 2024, I joined World Food Program, and it helped me to move from working from my home into buying more than one hectare of land. And now I produce 400 tons of organic fertilizer and 200 tons of animal feeds.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: And also, I thank the World Food Program because it grows my team from 23 workers up to 80 workers. Now I am happy because I provide training in three districts, mostly in Nyanza, Gisagara, and Musanze district through the World Food Program support. While today we have a growing demand of markets, we serve only 60% of farmers, while 90% of farmers need our fertilizer regionally.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: To unlock this opportunity, we want 50,000 USD to grow our market demand and expand our training opportunity to farmers. Please join Amazing Insects Limited to prove that youth are an agent of change. Please join us to buy from youth and support youth.

segments.speaker: Josiane · Amazing Insects
segments.text: Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you so much, Josiane. Thank you so much for those inspiring words, and then also the welcome to buy from youth.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: As we heard of this incredible pitch from innovators and the entrepreneurs' ambitions, let's again give them a round of applause, please. Let's give them another round of applause, because they did an amazing job, and I hope you understand and then had the business mindset while listening to them. We are going to have a next short session, where we are going to hear from the experts.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Experts are the people who are in the room, from financial institutions, organizations that work with agri-food systems, youth and women. But before, help me to connect that with calling WFP, country representative, to come and then set the scene for that, and then give us a remark while he's introducing dreams to deals, which is going to be our next session. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Honourable Minister of State for Youth at Heart, Honourable Under-Secretary for Youth Support from South Sudan, Honourable Minister for Youth Empowerment from Ghana, representative from the Government of Rwanda, colleagues from the UN, partners, and many youth, young entrepreneurs across Africa. Good afternoon, bonjour, and miri weneza. Thank you to the YouthConnekt Africa Summit team and the Government of Rwanda, a old partner from bringing us together.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: We share a goal, to help young people turn their idea into strong businesses. To the youth entrepreneurs who just shared your story and you pitch your business, thank you for showing us what you are building and where you want to go next. Your pitches showed us what is possible.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: The question now is what it takes to turn the promise into a lasting business. Young entrepreneurs need to know what customers want, have access to finance, and find buyers who will come back again and again. At WFP and FAO, we see what happens when young entrepreneurs get the support.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: In Rwanda, and in seven countries over Africa, Shoranesa, our partnership with Mastercard Foundation, is reaching more than 800,000 young people. More than 400,000 say they have found dignified and fulfilling work. The lesson is clear.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: Training and business support work best when they help young people meet real demand. Customers can be large companies, small local businesses, or young people themselves. When a business grows, it can open doors for others in the community.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: We see the value of connection in the sales they generate. Through Shoranesa, WFP has helped connect businesses with buyers, leading to more than 1.5 million in transactions. So, to the buyer, to the bank, the partners here today, I have one question.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: What can you do to help a young entrepreneur understand the market, win a customer, and secure the funding to grow? That is the question at the heart of our conversation, from dream to deals. We will hear from organizations that work with young entrepreneurs. Let's focus on what they can offer, how entrepreneurs can reach customers, and what each of us can do next.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: And please, let's keep the conversation going after this session. Exchange contact details, share your knowledge, and explore business partnership with a young entrepreneur that you heard from today. Young people need more than training.

segments.speaker: WFP Representative in Rwanda
segments.text: They need buyers who are ready to do business for them. So, let's turn today's idea into action. Let's partner with youth, let's buy from youth, and let's invest in youth.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you so much, Andrea, WFP representative in Rwanda. We are going to, I'm going to call on the gender and inclusion specialist to come and then moderate this last session, which is about from dreams to deals.

segments.speaker: Session hosts · Claire Muneza (FAO) and Jessy Lafourcade (AFSF)
segments.text: So, we are coming, we heard about the dreams, we heard about the pitches, but now let's see if we can get the deals here. Thank you, Lenarda, the floor is yours. A round of applause for Lenarda, please.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you. Honorable ministers, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon. I know time is not on our favor, but I will try to be very fast to make sure that people are going for lunch, you'll bear with us at least, let's secure a few minutes to complete the session.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: So, you have heard from youth, you realize that doing business, especially in the agri-food system as a youth, it's doable, but it requires more than just an idea, and that's why today we invited experts from different institutions that have what your youth need to make sure that your businesses can grow even further. So, without further ado, I will call them, and please, you will join our hands together, they are coming on the stage. To start with, we have the Vice Chancellor for Rwanda Institute of Conservation Agriculture, Dr. Mumumal Jeyang.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Welcome on stage. As he's coming on the stage, we also have the Managing Director, we have the Managing Director for Africa Food System Forum, Pate Sen. Welcome on stage.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Third, we have the Executive Secretary for Equity Group Foundation, Madam Roy Svamini. Welcome. We also have a representative from BRD, or Development Bank of Rwanda, Ujistenda Tavae.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: You're welcome on stage as well. And last but not least, we have a representative from Access to Finance Rwanda. His name is Martin Karinzi.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Welcome on stage as well. Okay, thank you so much, our panelists, for honoring our invitation. We really appreciate that.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Before we start, we are running out of time, as you can see, so I kindly request everyone to keep your responses brief and precise so that we can let people go for lunch. To start with, we had youth talking about challenges, where they started from, and where they are today. But we realized that youth need practical skills.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: They need reliable buyers. They need investment. They need financing.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: They need linkages to the market to ensure that their businesses are growing. So I'll start with you, Dr. Dieng, for the skills part. Just briefly, because you have heard what youth there – you have heard what youth already mentioned, shared with other stories.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: I want you to – like, kind of giving them a brief feedback on what they are going through from where they started and where they are now and how they can improve, but also bring it into the perspective of skills, of what IRCA is providing, to make sure that these youth are – because they want reliable buyers, but they should also be reliable suppliers. Thank you. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: So those were amazing presentations, and they really embody what we try to convey and share with young people at IRCA. What I heard from the presentation is that you should, for instance, look for the customers before the capital, right? That's really important. That's one of the first lessons in entrepreneurship, really.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: Another lesson that was very evident in the presentation was that you need to think about the problem before the product. It's easy to come up with a solution and then start looking for clients and customers, but really you need to start with the problem, and I think that many of the presenters really illustrated that. And then maybe the last one that I will draw from the presentation is that you need to start small.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: Many of those presenters told us about how they started gradually, so there's nothing wrong with starting small. Starting small is not the same thing as thinking small, right? You can start small but still think big. So these are three of the lessons that I drew from the presentation, and to go back to your question about skills, this is really what IRCA is about.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: IRCA is the Rwanda Institute for Conservation Agriculture. We really – I would not call us a university. In fact, we like to think of ourselves as a forum that functions as a university, not the other way around, right? We are a very, very experiential learning institution, so we don't sit in classrooms and think about the hypothetical ideal forum.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: We are on a forum trying to make it work and drawing lessons for that as a university. And so our experiential model is what we are really proud of. Our students learn by doing.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: Very early on from their first year, they are confronted with the same problem as smallholder farmers are confronted in Rwanda and elsewhere on the continent. So they start in small teams of seven, just like a small smallholder farmer unit. They are given a field, and then they have to make decisions about what to produce, how to spend money, how to use limited resources, how to keep financial records that are accurate and reliable and things of that sort.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: And then as they move through the program at RICA, then they get into a bigger team that is more like a village, right? So it's in the confines of their residence hall. And then later on in the program, the whole cohort gets together and gets a bigger field to manage. And the idea is that they move slowly through what it's like to be a smallholder farmer, then a bigger operation, and eventually a commercial operation.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: And so it's very much like what here in Rwanda you would see as the Fobases, right? These clusters of villages. We try to put our students in exactly the same conditions, having to solve exactly the same problems and make the same tough decisions, right? And so once they finish that, then they go into really more of commercial training. We are lucky, thanks to the generosity of both the government of Rwanda and the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, to have really state-of-the-art facilities.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: So we are able to expose our students to the entire agricultural value chain using really amazing equipment. So we expose them to what it's like to do food processing at a commercial level. They produce their own milk and cheese.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: They are able to increase the production of cattle, right? They are able to actually manage their own livestock, and so on and so forth, until the last year, when we allow them now to start ventures. And I'm very proud to say that we see the results of this really experiential approach that we have. One of our graduates, Axel Mizero, actually recently won the World Food Challenge Prize in Rome, Italy, thanks to the innovation that she came up with throughout this process that I just described.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: She was able to create a heat-resistant strain of mushrooms, and her project was to fight protein deficiency, to be able to solve the issue of protein availability in Rwanda. So she was able to develop a new strain of mushroom that was recognized worldwide as the overall global prize winner for the World Food Challenge Program. And that shows really that this experiential approach is really about being able to put students in positions to solve problems.

segments.speaker: Dr. Momar Dieng · Vice Chancellor, RICA
segments.text: We don't want to just have graduates who know about agriculture. We want them to see problems and put themselves in a position to see those problems in agriculture as opportunities and invitations for innovation and run with it. Thank you so much, Dr. Jiang, for inspiration, experience you're sharing, because this is answering the question that people who work in youth employment that always we come across like, are skills being given in academic institution match what is required at the market place? So thank you so much for sharing that.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: This is bringing me back to you, Pate. I know Africa Food System Forum is a huge platform that acts as a marketing linkages for youth, for people, different groups in agri-food system. So briefly as well, you can share what you can contribute to this youth, like, what do you think they need for their business to grow further, but also sharing what Africa Food System Forum has to offer to them.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you very much.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: And it was great also to be here and hearing all these fantastic projects and ideas. So let me start by saying, you know, one of the speaker, I think it's Israel, who said, I'm trying to find a solution to our problem, community. Wherever you are, do not start a business by something just you like.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: You may like it, but there is no market for you. And most of the mistake we do as entrepreneurs in Africa, you like something because it's your hobby, and then you do it. And then later when it dies, because nobody buy.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: Start always with the market. What's the market wants? What's the problem? And when a problem is in a community, people are ready to buy the service, are ready to buy the goods, are ready to buy an idea. So as simple as that.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: And so our young entrepreneurs sometimes also compare to yourself to Silicon Valley, you know, where innovation is happening. Most of those innovation, when it happens, you see the market of the US and people who are rich buying. So the next step is like scale up and they became billionaires because that solution is a problem for global humanity.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: And at the end of the day, it should not be just your small community, but it's a scale so you can take it to the region, to a country, to a continent, to the world. So at the moment you come from looking the solution from a problem perspective, then you start getting to a market. Second point.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: So buy from youth. I strongly believe we need quota from government perspective. If we have programs in different countries and we say these are innovators, they were awarded, everybody knows that these solutions are working.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: Let's take from a national budget and say, if there we have X number of innovators in this country, the national budget will allocate X amount of money to do local procurement from them. And it became a quota and it's a policy. And that helped all those young innovators that start with ideas to get also public procurement from a government and others will follow.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: Because at the end of the day, public procurement helped. The third point, just to come to the Africa Food System Forum, and I will end there because of time. So we have this platform where at the end of the day, there is no lack of money in this world.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: People are sitting on their money, but they want the risk investment. So if it is too risky, they won't get in. The moment you start thinking about your business, look at all risk.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: It's political, environmental, fiduciary, financial, all those type of risk. And as you are close to your project, you know better the risk than anyone. Do not hide them.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: Get them back and forth and look at it and put all those risks. From that risk perspective, when it's low, obviously, even if you ask your brother or whoever else who don't know you that come and invest, they will invest. So I think these are elements which need to be looked at.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: And please reinvest also your money into your business. The first investor is not necessarily the market, but it's you. And the moment you start making money, get into it.

segments.speaker: Amath Pathé Sene · Managing Director, AFSF
segments.text: So what we'll do in the Africa Food System Forum, all these projects presented this year, we are going to take them back to this platform, where most of them we have this kind of like, you know, investors and then help this one to refine it. There are some sections that could be refined, but again, scalability cannot be just a project for a small, but if it works in Rwanda, it should work in Chad, it should work in Mali and another country. So if that's the case, then we get scale and then the project became a big one.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you. Okay. Thank you so much for sharing that.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: I like the point that you mentioned about the risks. So this brings me to a question that I want to ask Royce, because for financial institutions, whenever we ask them, because you always share, there are different products for youth and women, but when we ask or analyze deeply, we learn from you that, yes, products are there, but we invest where there is low risk and quick returns. And yes, that is a fact because it's a business, but reflecting on pictures we had from youth, I want you to share with them the, yes, the experience of the bank, like the issues that you always see that youth have, why money is there, but they are not getting money, what is lacking, and also maybe the products or the advantages they are not aware of.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Leonarda.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: And that is a very important question. Listening to the youth pitching this morning, I could see that financial institutions are the ones that can be able to connect the dots and take out the mismatch that is happening in terms of investments. So, answering your question, let me start it from the data that we have.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: Today, we have Finescope report 2024, and it shows us that 94 percent of the youth in Rwanda are financially included, but 18 percent are banked. So, for me, that is a very big highlight. It speaks to a lot of things, and it actually speaks to the comment that was made by the Director General from the Ministry of Agriculture, mentioning that supporting the youth is not charity, but an obligation by all the stakeholders.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: So, when we think about 18 percent of the youth in Rwanda being the only percentage banked, that poses a real challenge, and it shows that what you're mentioning is actually happening. So, what is the issue? Banks have always said money is there, and the young entrepreneurs have ideas, as we were saying. So, what is the missing link between the available funds in the market and supporting entrepreneurs to be able to grow their business and scale? So, the biggest challenge is what you started off with, the risks.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: The risks exist, but it doesn't mean that banks cannot finance the youth, because as much as there are risks, especially in agriculture, there are also the risking instruments in the market, and their partners, as Pate just mentioned, that money is there. People are sitting on money. All we need is to come together, bring different ideas, and be able to support agri-entrepreneurs, to support the youth, to be able to put their ideas into real goods.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: So, speaking on behalf of Equity Bank, I'm here representing the MD of Equity Bank, because I lead the foundation. Equity Bank has really taken a very intentional move in terms of supporting the youth, and the move does not only focus on money, but it has understood that financing should not move in isolation, but it should be matched with real market opportunities and skills. What does this mean? The intentionality has been put in two ways.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: First of all, let's start by building the foundation. Let's start by supporting the youth. Let's start by supporting the smallholder farmers.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: And how do we support them? We support them by establishing the foundation, which is a non-for-profit, and the focus of the foundation is to build capacities, specifically around financial literacy, education, specifically around entrepreneurship. And in addition to that, we do market linkages, but we also crowd in partners to make sure that we attain the risking instruments that can be able to serve the young entrepreneurs. So, that is one side.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: Number two is the bank. Given that the bank understands the challenges in the market, looks at statistics and interprets them, and is intentional to support the youth, different financial products have been developed, and these are products that have been developed to answer the challenges that we have in the market. We have specifically tailored products for the youth, especially in agriculture, for women in agriculture.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: We have different products focusing on youth groups, the VSLAs. If we look at our rural communities, most of the youth, women, and smallholder farmers are organized into groups which are called village savings and lending associations. Those are usually considered as informal groups, but these are very productive groups.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: It is a very great model that has worked in rural areas, and therefore, based on that, the bank has come up with a financial product that is able to respond to their needs. And specifically, these products, which are tailored to the youth, to women, to VSLAs, are collateral free, and we understand that that has been the biggest challenge in the market. So, that is what the bank has done.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: But in addition to that, the bank has looked at traditional banking to be a big challenge and a big barrier that is actually causing the statistics to be still at 18%. And therefore, the bank has rolled out a digital solution called Equity Mobile Money Africa. It is a digital platform where different people will enroll.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: They will use their smartphones to borrow, to transact, to pay their bills, to separate their business cash flows and their personal funds, and therefore, it also ultimately helps them to be able to build limits for loans that they can be able to access. So, Coratto and other traditional barriers are not going to be a problem anymore, because once you enroll on that platform, you transact, then you're able to build a loan for yourself. Number two, in terms of digitization, for those who are in agriculture specifically, all the entrepreneurs that came here to speak are specifically innovators in agriculture.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: There's a subset of the digital system that is called Equifarm, and Equifarm is specifically for supporting agriculture and entrepreneurs. How it is structured, it is a closed-loop system. It is helping farmers to be linked to anchors.

segments.speaker: Equity Bank representative
segments.text: I had some of the entrepreneurs speaking about data, about MCCs, milk correction, aggregators, supporting farmers. So, those are the people that are being onboarded on that platform to be able to support their farmers to access inputs, to access finance, and to penetrate the market without really any Coratto requirement or any other challenges in the market. So, I think those are the main ones that I can highlight in respect to the challenges that we've seen.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thanks. Thank you so much, Lois. I can see there is a lot to share.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Let this platform not be the end. We will have even more platforms to explore more opportunities. Justine, you heard what Roy shared.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: One thing, a big number having access to finance, but a very slight number is their products or their businesses are bankable. So, I don't know if you're, I think you have the same problem or the same challenge, but again, we would like to learn how BRD is supporting youth and how you ensure that you have those instruments that are de-risking to the extent that you can manage to support youth, especially those in agri-food system. Please, let us be precise and get on the point.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you for the opportunity to speak. I think mine is going to be brief since my fellow panelists have spoken about the solutions that are there.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: I like the fact that the colleagues talked about scalability and the innovation. Today, we are talking on linkage to the market, but also like the fact that the presenters, the ones who came here to pitch their project covered the entire value chain in the agri-sector from land preparation, input, up to the stage of linkage to the market. But mine is going to be brief.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: I'm just going to talk about the solutions that are local, that are existing, and maybe guide the project promoters on how they can access them. Now, talking from a banking point of view, you kept talking about BRD. For the interest of the audience, BRD is Development Bank of Rwanda.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: As my colleague Lloyd said, we have products, customized products that have been put on the market to meet the needs from this project that our young fellows are presenting. So, the doctor talked about the market and the risk associated to the product. As long as there is a market, I don't think any project that has been presented can be financially viable.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: How do we reach that stage of going to the market? It's about equipping the promoters. One, conducting a market research, being innovative on what you need to do as a project owner, but also conducting the market before you set the product to the market. So, when it comes to the risk from the perspective of the bank, a bank has products from the perspective of BRD.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: We have loans, loans that have been, we grant loans with a long tenor that are customized to investments specific in the agri-sectors, but we also grant a rest period for the project promoters to have enough time to start collecting cash flows from their project and before they can start repaying the loans. In addition to those loans that we grant, by the way, loans that have concessional pricing, because we know investing in this sector, it requires enough time to start generating high income, high margin, so that you can meet financial obligations as an investor. In addition to loans that the bank grants to the market, we also have this de-risking instrument that she talked about.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: We know that most of these young entrepreneurs, most of the time they start their project without having collaterals, and traditional banking requires some collateralization for the loans that they grant to these entrepreneurs. So, we have a bank guarantee that supports these entrepreneurs, and when it comes to youth, they have a special treatment that embeds incentives in terms of the level of collateralization. But when it comes also to linking them to the market, we have these advisory services that we have a team dedicated with providing, equipping the entrepreneurs with the right skills to run their businesses.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: We also have technical assistance that we deploy to the market to support all these good ideas that they have, to scale them, and not only to supply the local market, but to outsource off the contract from abroad. I think in a nutshell now, I think the audience would like to know how they access those products and services. As BRB, for us, we work with all the financial institutions operating in the country.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: For this specific segment of the clientele, for the youth, we have partnerships with the district circles across the entire countries. So, all this money that I'm talking about, the jurisdictions, so we have this partnership with the district circles, so they have branches across the entire country. From where you operate, please go to any circle branch, inquire about this product that we are talking about, but also feel free to reach out to BRB from where we are at the head office.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you. Thank you so much, Riste, for sharing all those products. Youth who are here, I think you're recording, I think from here, you can reach to circles in your district, and even Marthe will be, I mean, Riste will be out there as he's going out, you can go and ask him for more details if you want, but don't let these opportunities go without getting something.

segments.speaker: BRD representative
segments.text: Money is not a problem, but strategies to have that money is required. One comment. We also have staff representatives down there, BRB staff representatives, for anyone willing to get more inquiries from the team, you can meet them.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Okay, thank you. I'm coming to you, Marthe, from Access to Finance Rwanda. You heard from youth as well.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: You have ideas, because when we're about Access to Finance Rwanda, you saw some people think that you go there, you get money, but the terms and conditions apply, and you need to follow the regulations and everything, so please share with youth how Access to Finance Rwanda is supporting youth projects and work and everything, briefly. Thank you. Thank you so much.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: Thank you to you, to the organizers, and to the youth that is attending here. I'm here representing our CEO, Kameta Sainzoga, our CEO of the Access to Finance Rwanda, who couldn't make it here. And Access to Finance Rwanda is actually, some people think we are the bank.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: Yeah, we are a not-for-profit company that is driving the financial inclusion for all in Rwanda, so we work with different partners, we work with the government of Rwanda, we work with development partners, we work with banks, we work with all the ecosystem players, who play a role to make sure financial services are as inclusive as possible. There was one young woman, I wrote down her name, she's called Claudine, she asked a question if we see youth as a risk, and I wanted to quickly say no. We really see these young entrepreneurs here as tomorrow's generation of suppliers, exporters, experts, like the fellow colleagues we have here, so we really don't see them as a risk.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: But at Access to Finance Rwanda, we also tried to put together interventions that may lead to de-risking anything that may be a constraint for the youth to access finance. So we have, actually we have also a booth downstairs in front of D12, I think, and youth can also go there and get enough information about our interventions, but I will talk about a few. First of all, we work with different banks in Rwanda in collaboration with different development partners, and we have a guarantee scheme that can cover up to 70 percent of the loan cover, which is, and the youth can also cover 30 percent remaining, so, and we work with different banks through that scheme.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: We have an interest rate subsidy, because also, apart from the collateral that has been an issue for youth, also interest rates, sometimes they say it's too much, and maybe it becomes a bit expensive as someone trying to grow. So we have an interest rate subsidy that covers eight percent of the interest rates, so for some particular value chains in agriculture, and more details can be shared at our booth on how to access them through our partner financial service providers. We also have a credit-linked subsidy, which is a matching grant, so once an SME has secured a loan, they want, we match it with a grant, and then, and this is also done through partner banks for some particular value chains in agribusiness.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: Apart from that, I think, as my fellow panelists said, for us to be able to help the businesses be ready for finance, we have a MSME facility that also supports MSMEs with finance readiness, so we facilitate MSMEs to access business development services that will respond to the issues that constrain them to access finance, so be it credit applications. Some people fail to get a credit because they can't even apply. They don't know the requirements, or even if they know, they don't know how to meet them.

segments.speaker: Access to Finance Rwanda representative
segments.text: We help them with the credit applications, we prepare them for that, and we help them with post-credit management so that they can be able to manage their loans, and we also try to link them with all of these opportunities that fellow panelists mentioned here, so we work closely with some of them and other ecosystem players. One quick advice, youth and agripreneurs work together, please, because also I think most of the buyers, they are trying to buy enough and consistent produce, but if you are trying to handle it alone, at some point you may not be able to satisfy them, but if you work together, you can make a great business. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Uwinkesha Lenarda · Panel moderator
segments.text: Thank you so much, Martin, as we are rounding up this session. I'm glad you gave them advice, so 30 seconds, everyone, your advice is there, then commitment. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.
One last comment from me for the youth. For those who have started, congratulations, but the journey is still long. The new ones come to us.
We are here to support you. It's our mandate. Let's work hard.
Let's feel exhausted. We enjoy the fruit tomorrow. Thank you.

Thank you. Lois? Mine is really to appreciate the opportunity to come and speak to my young sisters and brothers this afternoon. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you very much.

As I said earlier, I think a piece of advice is find a problem before you start building a product, and find your customers before you try to find capital, and learn by doing, and if you want to do that, RICA is the best place to do that. As I said, we are a firm that works as a university, not the other way around, so we look forward to welcoming you. Come see our beautiful campus and see how sustainable agriculture is supposed to be done.
Africa is a land of opportunity. Our youth, they are the seed of opportunities. Try, fail, try again, try, try.
Dream big and never give up, and we make our continent proud. Thank you so much, our partner. Okay, okay.

segments.text: Thank you so much, Louise, and thank you so much, our panelists. We really appreciate your time and for honoring our invitation, your partners we need, and let's collaborate and make sure youth employment in the food system is strengthened. Thank you.
